messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is an eighteen-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a junior tax consultant at a small accounting firm in Atlanta. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, seeking help for the first time approximately four months after being raped by a male colleague at a work social event. The assault occurred in a back office of the venue after Kofi had stepped away from the group. The door was pulled shut behind them. There was shouting — his attacker's voice raised and commanding — and then, when Kofi tried to call out, a hand clamped over his mouth. He remembers the taste of sweat and something metallic, the image of fluorescent light overhead, and then a long period in which sensation continued but coherent thought did not. When it was over, the door opened and the man walked out as though nothing had happened.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi told no one. He returned to work, sat at his desk, and processed tax filings. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt like knowledge rather than fear, that he had failed to protect himself in some fundamental way, and that disclosing what had happened would confirm this failure to everyone around him. The office, where he spends most of his waking hours, became the primary theatre of his distress. Male colleagues passing his cubicle, the ordinary percussion of doors opening and closing down the hallway, a raised voice from a phone call in the next room — each of these now carries the sensory signature of the assault, and when they occur, Kofi's nervous system responds as though the event is recurring. His heart rate spikes, his chest tightens, and he scans the room with a vigilance that exhausts him by midday. Being alone with any male colleague — even briefly, even in a glass-walled conference room — produces a level of alarm that he struggles to conceal behind the posture of professional composure.

These triggers do not merely frighten him in the present; they pull him backward. When a door slams in the hallway, the fluorescent image returns — sharp, uninvited, arriving as a picture before it arrives as a thought. Sometimes there is no image at all, only the full emotional weight of that night pressing down on him without context, a wave of terror and shame that he cannot locate in any specific memory and therefore cannot reason his way out of. Most disorienting of all is the taste: something metallic and organic that surfaces without warning, most often when he is sitting quietly at his desk, and that makes the past feel physically present in a way that no amount of logical reassurance can undo. These intrusive returns of the memory, in turn, make the triggers more potent — each recurrence deepens his association between ordinary sensory events and catastrophic harm, so that sounds and presences that once meant nothing now mean everything.

The heightened threat he feels in his body has its own momentum. When he is already in a state of alarm — heart up, muscles braced — any new sensory input is processed through that lens, and the memories come faster and more vividly. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a supervisor, meant kindly, sent him out of the office and into the stairwell for twenty minutes. He has stopped attending team lunches. He no longer takes client meetings that are not in open, familiar spaces, and he has begun declining assignments that require site visits, telling his manager he is managing his workload. He avoids any unfamiliar location because, as he puts it, he cannot read the exits, cannot assess who else might be there, cannot know in advance whether he will be safe. Strangers approaching him on the street — even in the most ordinary circumstances, a pedestrian asking for directions — register as threats before he has time to evaluate them rationally. His world has quietly contracted.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a performance review in which his manager noted his increasing withdrawal and asked, gently, whether something was wrong. He said nothing in that meeting, but he made the appointment the following day. What he is most afraid of is that the person he was before that night no longer exists. What he is most hoping for is some way to sit in his own office without feeling like it is still happening.
